source.name: FIFO Depth Calculation Made Easy (Putta Satish)

questions.title: What is the general method for calculating FIFO depth, and why can a FIFO only absorb bursty (not continuous) traffic?
questions.answer: FIFO depth = number of data items left unread at the end of the write burst. FIFO only works for bursts; continuous faster writes need infinite depth.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** The FIFO must hold every item that is written but not yet read during the burst: depth = items written in the burst window - items the reader can drain in that same window. If writes are faster than reads forever, no finite depth works.

| Step | What you compute |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Effective write period T_w = (idle_w + 1) / f_A (time per written item) |
| 2 | Burst write time T_burst = B x T_w |
| 3 | Effective read period T_r = (idle_r + 1) / f_B |
| 4 | Items read during the burst N_r = floor(T_burst / T_r) |
| 5 | Depth = B - N_r (then add sync margin, round up to 2^n) |

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk_A", "wave": "p..........."}, {"name": "wr_en", "wave": "01.......0.."}, {"name": "rd_en", "wave": "0.1010101010"}, {"name": "level", "wave": "=.==========", "data": ["0", "1", "1", "2", "2", "3", "3", "4", "4", "3", "3"]}], "head": {"text": "write burst fills faster than reads drain; level peaks at the end of the burst"}}
```

### Explanation
- A FIFO is a rate-matching buffer: it is needed when the producer is temporarily faster than the consumer.
- The peak occupancy happens at the moment the last item of the burst is written; that peak is the minimum depth.
- If the average write rate exceeds the average read rate over an unbounded time, occupancy grows without bound, so you need flow control (back-pressure), not a deeper FIFO.
- Ask the interviewer for: f_A, f_B, burst length, idle cycles (or enable duty cycles), and the gap between bursts (it must be long enough to drain).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Use the reader's rate *during the burst window*, not over the whole period.
- Round items read **down** (a partially completed read does not free an entry).
- Depth also needs margin for pointer-synchronizer latency in an async FIFO.

### Follow-ups
- *Would you round the depth up to a power of two?* Yes for an async FIFO with Gray pointers (e.g. 45 -> 64), because Gray-code pointer wrap only works cleanly for 2^n depths.
- *What about synchronizer latency?* The full/empty flags are seen 2-3 destination cycles late, so add a few entries of margin on top of the computed number.
- *What is the closed-form?* Depth = B - B x (T_w / T_r) = B x (1 - rate_r / rate_w), rounded up.

questions.title: FIFO depth: writer at 80 MHz, reader at 50 MHz, burst of 120 items, no idle cycles on either side. What is the minimum depth?
questions.prompt: f_A (write) = 80 MHz, f_B (read) = 50 MHz, burst length = 120, no idle cycles on write or read.
questions.answer: Write 1 item = 12.5 ns, burst = 1500 ns. Read 1 item = 20 ns -> 75 read in 1500 ns. Depth = 120 - 75 = 45.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Write time for the burst = 120 x 12.5 ns = 1500 ns; in 1500 ns the reader drains 1500/20 = 75 items, so 120 - 75 = **45** entries must be buffered.

| Time (ns) | Written (every 12.5 ns) | Read (every 20 ns) | Occupancy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 100 | 8 | 5 | 3 |
| 500 | 40 | 25 | 15 |
| 1000 | 80 | 50 | 30 |
| 1500 (burst ends) | 120 | 75 | **45 (peak)** |
| 2400 | 120 | 120 | 0 (drained) |

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk_A 80MHz", "wave": "p..........."}, {"name": "wr_en", "wave": "01.........."}, {"name": "clk_B 50MHz", "wave": "p..........."}, {"name": "rd_en", "wave": "0.1........."}, {"name": "level", "wave": "=.=.=.=.=.=.", "data": ["0", "1", "2", "3", "4", "5"]}], "head": {"text": "back-to-back writes and reads; level grows by 3 every 100 ns (8 writes vs 5 reads)"}}
```

### Explanation
- T_w = 1/80 MHz = 12.5 ns, T_r = 1/50 MHz = 20 ns.
- Burst time = 120 x 12.5 = 1500 ns.
- Reads in 1500 ns = 1500 / 20 = 75.
- Depth = 120 - 75 = **45**.
- Closed form: 120 x (1 - 50/80) = 120 x 0.375 = 45.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Do not use the reader's time to read 120 items (2400 ns); the peak occurs at 1500 ns when the writer stops.
- A practical async FIFO would be 64 deep (power of two plus sync margin).

### Follow-ups
- *Would you round the depth up to a power of two?* Yes for an async FIFO with Gray pointers (e.g. 45 -> 64), because Gray-code pointer wrap only works cleanly for 2^n depths.
- *What about synchronizer latency?* The full/empty flags are seen 2-3 destination cycles late, so add a few entries of margin on top of the computed number.

questions.title: FIFO depth: f_A = 80 MHz > f_B = 50 MHz, burst of 120, with "one clock cycle delay between two successive reads and writes". How does this change the answer?
questions.prompt: f_A = 80 MHz, f_B = 50 MHz, burst = 120, one clock cycle delay between two successive reads and between two successive writes.
questions.answer: Same as the no-idle case: one cycle between successive transfers = back-to-back. Depth = 45.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** It does not change anything: "one clock between successive transfers" just means one transfer per clock (back-to-back), identical to the no-idle case, so depth = **45**.

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk_A", "wave": "p........"}, {"name": "wr_en", "wave": "01......."}, {"name": "wdata", "wave": "x=======x", "data": ["D0", "D1", "D2", "D3", "D4", "D5", "D6"]}], "head": {"text": "successive writes are one clock apart = zero idle cycles"}}
```

| Wording | Items per clock | Equivalent idle cycles |
| --- | --- | --- |
| no idle cycles | 1 | 0 |
| one clock delay between successive writes | 1 | 0 |
| one idle cycle between writes | 1/2 | 1 |

### Explanation
- The time between the start of transfer *n* and transfer *n+1* is one clock period, i.e. continuous streaming.
- So T_w = 12.5 ns, T_r = 20 ns, burst = 1500 ns, reads = 75, depth = 120 - 75 = **45**.
- The question is a wording trap: distinguish "delay of one cycle between transfers" (period = 1 clk) from "one idle cycle between transfers" (period = 2 clk).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Clarify the spec with the interviewer: say out loud which interpretation you use and show both numbers if unsure (45 vs 83 for 1 idle write / 3 idle read).

### Follow-ups
- *Would you round the depth up to a power of two?* Yes for an async FIFO with Gray pointers (e.g. 45 -> 64), because Gray-code pointer wrap only works cleanly for 2^n depths.
- *What about synchronizer latency?* The full/empty flags are seen 2-3 destination cycles late, so add a few entries of margin on top of the computed number.

questions.title: FIFO depth: f_A = 80 MHz, f_B = 50 MHz, burst of 120, 1 idle cycle between writes and 3 idle cycles between reads. Minimum depth?
questions.prompt: f_A = 80 MHz, f_B = 50 MHz, burst = 120, idle cycles between writes = 1, idle cycles between reads = 3.
questions.answer: T_w = 25 ns, burst = 3000 ns; T_r = 80 ns -> 37 reads. Depth = 120 - 37 = 83.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** One write every 2 clk_A cycles (25 ns) and one read every 4 clk_B cycles (80 ns). Burst lasts 120 x 25 = 3000 ns, reader completes floor(3000/80) = 37 reads, so depth = 120 - 37 = **83**.

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk_A", "wave": "p..........."}, {"name": "wr_en", "wave": "010101010101"}, {"name": "clk_B", "wave": "p..........."}, {"name": "rd_en", "wave": "010001000100"}], "head": {"text": "write: 1 of every 2 clk_A cycles; read: 1 of every 4 clk_B cycles"}}
```

| Quantity | Value |
| --- | --- |
| T_w = 2 / 80 MHz | 25 ns |
| Burst time = 120 x 25 | 3000 ns |
| T_r = 4 / 50 MHz | 80 ns |
| Reads in 3000 ns = 3000/80 = 37.5 | 37 complete reads |
| Depth = 120 - 37 | **83** |

### Explanation
- Idle cycles stretch the effective period: (idle + 1) clock periods per item.
- Write rate = 40 Mitems/s, read rate = 12.5 Mitems/s; the gap is much larger than in the no-idle case.
- 37.5 is rounded **down** to 37 because half a read does not free an entry; that gives the safe (larger) depth 83.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Rounding 37.5 up to 38 would under-size the FIFO by one entry (82).
- Use 128 for a power-of-two async FIFO.

### Follow-ups
- *Would you round the depth up to a power of two?* Yes for an async FIFO with Gray pointers (e.g. 45 -> 64), because Gray-code pointer wrap only works cleanly for 2^n depths.
- *What about synchronizer latency?* The full/empty flags are seen 2-3 destination cycles late, so add a few entries of margin on top of the computed number.

questions.title: FIFO depth: f_A = 80 MHz, f_B = 50 MHz, burst of 120, wr_en duty cycle 50% and rd_en duty cycle 25%. Minimum depth?
questions.prompt: f_A = 80 MHz, f_B = 50 MHz, burst = 120, duty cycle of wr_en = 50%, duty cycle of rd_en = 25%.
questions.answer: Equivalent to 1 idle write cycle and 3 idle read cycles -> depth 83. (Source typo: second duty cycle refers to rd_en.)
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A 50% wr_en duty cycle means one write every 2 clk_A cycles and a 25% rd_en duty cycle means one read every 4 clk_B cycles: the same as the 1-idle/3-idle case, so depth = **83**.

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk_A", "wave": "p..........."}, {"name": "wr_en (50%)", "wave": "101010101010"}, {"name": "clk_B", "wave": "p..........."}, {"name": "rd_en (25%)", "wave": "100010001000"}], "head": {"text": "duty cycle of an enable = fraction of clocks carrying a transfer"}}
```

| Spec form | Write period | Read period |
| --- | --- | --- |
| idle cycles 1 / 3 | 2 clk_A = 25 ns | 4 clk_B = 80 ns |
| duty cycle 50% / 25% | 2 clk_A = 25 ns | 4 clk_B = 80 ns |

### Explanation
- Effective rate = f x duty: writes 80 x 0.5 = 40 M/s, reads 50 x 0.25 = 12.5 M/s.
- Burst time = 120 / 40 M = 3000 ns; reads in that time = 3000 x 12.5 M = 37.5 -> 37.
- Depth = 120 - 37 = **83**.
- (The source lists the second duty cycle as wr_enb again; it is clearly rd_en.)

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Duty cycle only gives the *average* rate. If the 50% enable could be high for many consecutive cycles (e.g. high for 60 then low for 60), the worst case is a back-to-back burst: then use f_A directly and depth grows. Ask how the enable is distributed.

### Follow-ups
- *Would you round the depth up to a power of two?* Yes for an async FIFO with Gray pointers (e.g. 45 -> 64), because Gray-code pointer wrap only works cleanly for 2^n depths.
- *What about synchronizer latency?* The full/empty flags are seen 2-3 destination cycles late, so add a few entries of margin on top of the computed number.

questions.title: FIFO depth: writer clock slower than reader clock (f_A < f_B), no idle cycles on either side. What depth is needed?
questions.prompt: f_A < f_B, no idle cycles in write or read (one transfer per clock on each side).
questions.answer: Reader is faster -> no data accumulates; FIFO depth of 1 is sufficient (plus sync latency margin in practice).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** The reader drains faster than the writer fills, so occupancy never builds up: logically a **depth of 1** (a single holding register) is enough; in an async FIFO you still need a few entries to cover pointer-synchronization latency.

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk_A (slow)", "wave": "p......."}, {"name": "wr_en", "wave": "0101010."}, {"name": "clk_B (fast)", "wave": "p......."}, {"name": "rd_en", "wave": "0.101010"}, {"name": "level", "wave": "0101010."}], "head": {"text": "each item is read before the next one arrives: level stays at <= 1"}}
```

| Time | Event | Occupancy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| t0 | write D0 | 1 |
| t0 + T_B | read D0 | 0 |
| t0 + T_A | write D1 | 1 |
| ... | ... | <= 1 |

### Explanation
- Rate_write = f_A < Rate_read = f_B, so B - N_r <= 0 for any burst length.
- A single entry handles the clock-domain crossing.
- Real design: an async FIFO's empty flag is updated only after the write pointer passes a 2-FF synchronizer, so the reader cannot pop immediately. Depth must cover that round-trip latency (typically 4-8 entries) to keep the writer from stalling.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- If the writer is back-pressured by a slow full-flag update, throughput drops even though average rates match; size for latency, not just rate.

### Follow-ups
- *Would you round the depth up to a power of two?* Yes for an async FIFO with Gray pointers (e.g. 45 -> 64), because Gray-code pointer wrap only works cleanly for 2^n depths.
- *What about synchronizer latency?* The full/empty flags are seen 2-3 destination cycles late, so add a few entries of margin on top of the computed number.

questions.title: FIFO depth: f_A = 30 MHz (write), f_B = 50 MHz (read), burst of 120, 1 idle cycle between writes and 3 idle cycles between reads. Minimum depth?
questions.prompt: f_A = 30 MHz, f_B = 50 MHz, burst = 120, idle cycles between writes = 1, idle cycles between reads = 3.
questions.answer: T_w = 66.67 ns, burst = 8000 ns; T_r = 80 ns -> 100 reads; depth = 20.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Even though the read clock is faster, the idle cycles make the effective read rate (12.5 M/s) slower than the effective write rate (15 M/s). Burst = 120 x 66.67 ns = 8000 ns, reads = 8000/80 = 100, depth = **20**.

| Quantity | Value |
| --- | --- |
| T_w = 2 / 30 MHz | 66.67 ns (15 M items/s) |
| Burst time = 120 x 66.67 ns | 8000 ns |
| T_r = 4 / 50 MHz | 80 ns (12.5 M items/s) |
| Reads in 8000 ns | 8000 / 80 = 100 |
| Depth = 120 - 100 | **20** |

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk_A 30MHz", "wave": "p..........."}, {"name": "wr_en", "wave": "101010101010"}, {"name": "clk_B 50MHz", "wave": "p..........."}, {"name": "rd_en", "wave": "100010001000"}], "head": {"text": "compare effective rates, not raw clock frequencies"}}
```

### Explanation
- Effective write rate = 30 MHz / 2 = 15 M/s; effective read rate = 50 MHz / 4 = 12.5 M/s.
- Closed form: 120 x (1 - 12.5/15) = 120 x 1/6 = **20**.
- Lesson: "f_A < f_B" alone does not mean depth 1; always compare *effective* rates.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- The source labels this case "f_A < f_B" without stating f_A; the worked numbers use f_A = 30 MHz.

### Follow-ups
- *Would you round the depth up to a power of two?* Yes for an async FIFO with Gray pointers (e.g. 45 -> 64), because Gray-code pointer wrap only works cleanly for 2^n depths.
- *What about synchronizer latency?* The full/empty flags are seen 2-3 destination cycles late, so add a few entries of margin on top of the computed number.

questions.title: FIFO depth: f_A = f_B (e.g. both 30 MHz), burst of 120, no idle cycles. Is a FIFO needed, and how deep?
questions.prompt: f_A = f_B = 30 MHz, burst = 120, no idle cycles.
questions.answer: No FIFO if clocks have no phase difference; depth 1 if there is a phase difference.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Equal rates mean nothing accumulates. If the clocks are the same clock (no phase difference) no FIFO is needed; if they are asynchronous clocks of the same nominal frequency, a depth of **1** logically suffices (practically a small async FIFO to absorb sync latency and ppm drift).

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk_A", "wave": "p......."}, {"name": "wr_en", "wave": "01......"}, {"name": "wdata", "wave": "x=======", "data": ["D0", "D1", "D2", "D3", "D4", "D5", "D6"]}, {"name": "clk_B", "wave": "p......."}, {"name": "rd_en", "wave": "0.1....."}, {"name": "rdata", "wave": "x.======", "data": ["D0", "D1", "D2", "D3", "D4", "D5"]}], "head": {"text": "one in, one out per cycle: occupancy stays constant"}}
```

| Clock relationship | Needed buffering |
| --- | --- |
| same clock / same phase | none (direct register path) |
| same frequency, unknown phase | 1 entry logically; async FIFO in practice |
| same nominal frequency, ppm offset (plesiochronous) | elastic buffer sized for drift over the burst |

### Explanation
- Write rate = read rate, so B - N_r = 0 except for the initial offset.
- With a phase difference you still must cross clock domains safely; a single-entry handshake or a small async FIFO does that.
- For long streams between plesiochronous clocks (e.g. +/-100 ppm), drift accumulates: 120 items x 200 ppm is far below 1, but for packets of millions of items you need an elastic buffer with skip symbols.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- An async FIFO's empty flag lags the write by ~2-3 read clocks, so the reader starts late; to stream at full rate the FIFO must cover that latency (~4 entries).

### Follow-ups
- *Would you round the depth up to a power of two?* Yes for an async FIFO with Gray pointers (e.g. 45 -> 64), because Gray-code pointer wrap only works cleanly for 2^n depths.
- *What about synchronizer latency?* The full/empty flags are seen 2-3 destination cycles late, so add a few entries of margin on top of the computed number.

questions.title: FIFO depth: f_A = f_B = 50 MHz, burst of 120, 1 idle cycle between writes and 3 idle cycles between reads. Minimum depth?
questions.prompt: f_A = f_B = 50 MHz, burst = 120, idle cycles between writes = 1, idle cycles between reads = 3.
questions.answer: T_w = 40 ns, burst = 4800 ns; T_r = 80 ns -> 60 reads; depth = 60.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Same clock frequency but different duty: one write per 40 ns vs one read per 80 ns. Burst = 120 x 40 = 4800 ns; reads = 4800/80 = 60; depth = **60**.

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk (50MHz)", "wave": "p..........."}, {"name": "wr_en", "wave": "101010101010"}, {"name": "rd_en", "wave": "100010001000"}, {"name": "level", "wave": "=.=.=.=.=.=.", "data": ["1", "1", "2", "2", "3", "3"]}], "head": {"text": "every 4 clocks: 2 writes, 1 read -> level +1"}}
```

| Quantity | Value |
| --- | --- |
| T_w = 2 x 20 ns | 40 ns |
| Burst time = 120 x 40 | 4800 ns |
| T_r = 4 x 20 ns | 80 ns |
| Reads in 4800 ns | 60 |
| Depth = 120 - 60 | **60** |

### Explanation
- Write rate = 25 M/s, read rate = 12.5 M/s: the reader drains exactly half of the burst.
- Closed form: 120 x (1 - 12.5/25) = **60**.
- Equal clock frequency does not imply equal data rate; idle cycles/duty cycles decide.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- If both sides are on the same clock you could use a synchronous FIFO (no Gray pointers), and the depth need not be a power of two.

### Follow-ups
- *Would you round the depth up to a power of two?* Yes for an async FIFO with Gray pointers (e.g. 45 -> 64), because Gray-code pointer wrap only works cleanly for 2^n depths.
- *What about synchronizer latency?* The full/empty flags are seen 2-3 destination cycles late, so add a few entries of margin on top of the computed number.

questions.title: FIFO depth: writer delivers 80 data per 100 clocks (any 20 cycles idle, randomly placed), reader consumes 8 data per 10 clocks, same clock, burst size 160. Minimum depth?
questions.prompt: Writing data = 80 DATA / 100 clocks (20 idle cycles placed randomly). Outgoing data = 8 DATA / 10 clocks. Burst size = 160. Write and read frequencies are equal.
questions.answer: Worst case: 160 written in 160 consecutive cycles (back-to-back windows). Reads in 160 cycles = 128. Depth = 32.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Worst case is two back-to-back write windows: the 80 writes of window 1 placed at its end and the 80 writes of window 2 at its start give **160 writes in 160 consecutive clocks**. The reader takes only 160 x 8/10 = 128 in that time, so depth = 160 - 128 = **32**.

| Placement of the 20 idle cycles | Cycles to write 160 items |
| --- | --- |
| idle at start of both windows | 200 |
| idle at end of both windows | 200 |
| idle split 10/10 in each window | 180 |
| window 1 idle first, window 2 idle last (worst case) | **160** |
| idle in the middle of both windows | 200 |

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "window", "wave": "=...=...", "data": ["100 clocks", "100 clocks"]}, {"name": "wr_en", "wave": "0.1...0."}, {"name": "rd_en (8 of 10)", "wave": "1......."}, {"name": "burst", "wave": "x.=...x.", "data": ["160 writes in 160 clks"]}], "head": {"text": "worst case: 20 idle | 80 writes || 80 writes | 20 idle"}}
```

### Explanation
- Write side: 160 items in 160 clocks (rate 1/clk) in the worst case.
- Read side: 8 per 10 clocks -> 0.8/clk -> 128 items in 160 clocks.
- Depth = 160 - 128 = **32**.
- Always pick the *maximum* instantaneous write rate and the *minimum* read rate the spec allows.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- The read side can also be bursty (8 of 10 clocks); worst case it reads at the end of its window. Using floor over each 10-cycle window still gives 128 over 160 cycles, so 32 holds if the reader's windows align; a fully adversarial reader alignment can add up to 2 more entries, so a careful answer is 32-34 -> choose 34 or simply 64 (power of two).

### Follow-ups
- *Would you round the depth up to a power of two?* Yes for an async FIFO with Gray pointers (e.g. 45 -> 64), because Gray-code pointer wrap only works cleanly for 2^n depths.
- *What about synchronizer latency?* The full/empty flags are seen 2-3 destination cycles late, so add a few entries of margin on top of the computed number.

questions.title: FIFO depth: f(clk_A) = f(clk_B)/4, period(en_B) = 100 x period(clk_A), duty cycle(en_B) = 25%. A writes every clk_A cycle; B reads every clk_B cycle while en_B is high. How deep must the FIFO be to avoid overflow and underflow?
questions.prompt:
Frequency(clk_A) = frequency(clk_B) / 4
Period(en_B) = period(clk_A) x 100
Duty cycle(en_B) = 25%
questions.answer: Assume clk_B = 100 MHz, clk_A = 25 MHz. Burst = 100 items in 4000 ns. Reading is enabled for 1000 ns only; items written in the other 3000 ns = 3000/40 = 75. Depth = 75.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Pick numbers: clk_B = 100 MHz, clk_A = 25 MHz. In one en_B period (4000 ns) A writes 100 items; B can read only during the 1000 ns window. The 3000 ns with en_B low accumulates 3000/40 = **75** items, which is the minimum depth.

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk_A (25MHz)", "wave": "p..........."}, {"name": "wr (every clk_A)", "wave": "1..........."}, {"name": "en_B (25%)", "wave": "0........1.."}, {"name": "level", "wave": "=..=..=..=.=", "data": ["0", "25", "50", "75 peak", "0"]}], "head": {"text": "en_B low 3000 ns: 75 items pile up; en_B high 1000 ns: B (4x faster) drains 75 + 25 new"}}
```

| Interval | Writes (every 40 ns) | Reads (every 10 ns) | Level at end |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0-3000 ns, en_B = 0 | 75 | 0 | **75** |
| 3000-4000 ns, en_B = 1 | 25 | up to 100 | 0 |
| Per 4000 ns period | 100 | 100 | balanced |

### Explanation
- The burst length is implied: one en_B period = 100 clk_A cycles = 100 writes.
- Reader capacity in the window = 1000 ns / 10 ns = 100 = writes per period, so the system is balanced (no long-term growth).
- Worst-case occupancy is at the moment en_B rises: 75 items -> depth **75** (practically 128 for async Gray pointers, or 75 + sync margin).
- The source says "items read in 3000 ns = 3000/40"; it really means items *written* while reading is disabled.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- If en_B's high window can start at any phase relative to the writes, the answer is still 75 because the low phase is 3000 ns long.
- If clk_B were only 2x clk_A, the reader could not drain 100 items in 1000 ns and the FIFO would overflow regardless of depth.

### Follow-ups
- *Would you round the depth up to a power of two?* Yes for an async FIFO with Gray pointers (e.g. 45 -> 64), because Gray-code pointer wrap only works cleanly for 2^n depths.
- *What about synchronizer latency?* The full/empty flags are seen 2-3 destination cycles late, so add a few entries of margin on top of the computed number.
